title: Levels in a Tree
statement:
You get the root of a binary tree. Return how many levels it has: the number of nodes on the longest path from the root down to a leaf. A single node has 1 level; an empty tree has 0.

Trees are written in level order with null for a missing child: [6, 2, 9] is 6 with children 2 and 9. An empty tree is [].

examples.why: The longest path is 6 → 9 → 7 → 8. It turns left and then right, so following only left children (6 → 2) or only right children (6 → 9 → 11) stops short.
We count nodes, not edges. One node is one level.

constraints: The tree is at most 500 levels deep
hints: If you already knew how many levels the left subtree and the right subtree have, how many would the whole tree have?
The whole tree is one level (the root) on top of its deeper child. An empty subtree contributes 0.
Recursively: depth(node) = 1 + max(depth(left), depth(right)), with depth(null) = 0. Or walk level by level with a queue and count the levels.

explain.intuition:
Trees are made of smaller trees, so ask the children. If the left subtree is 3 levels deep and the right is 1, the whole tree is the root plus the deeper side: 4. The empty tree is 0 levels, which makes leaves come out as 1 automatically. That is depth-first search: go all the way down, and the answers flow back up.

The other way is to look at the tree in rows, like reading a nested DOM outline one indentation level at a time. Put the root in a queue, then repeatedly take out a full row and put in all its children. The number of rows you process is the depth. DFS is shorter to write; BFS never recurses, so it is the safe choice when the tree may be very deep, and it is the natural one when the question is about levels anyway.
steps: DFS: return 0 for a null node.
BFS alternative: start a queue with the root (if any) and levels = 0.
While the queue is not empty: note its current size, take out exactly that many nodes, push their children, and add 1 to levels.
pitfalls: Counting edges instead of nodes. A single node is 1 level here, not 0.
Returning 1 for a null child, so every leaf counts as 2.
In the BFS version, reading queue.length inside the loop while you push children. Save the row size before the loop, or you mix two levels into one.

complexity.space: O(h) for DFS, O(w) for BFS (h = height, w = widest level)

solutions.title: Recursive DFS
solutions.idea: A tree is one level deeper than its deeper child. An empty tree has depth 0.

solutions.title: BFS, one level at a time
solutions.idea: Process the queue in whole rows. Each row is one level, so count the rows.

solutions.title: Iterative DFS with an explicit stack
solutions.idea: Push (node, depth) pairs onto a stack and keep the largest depth seen. Same visits as the recursion, but the stack is yours, so depth is never limited by the call stack.

followups: Return the minimum depth instead: the number of nodes on the shortest path to a leaf. Why does a node with one child need care?
